lessons.title: Minor Pentatonic - Box 1
lessons.summary: The single most useful shape in rock and blues soloing. Five notes, one position, endless licks.
steps: First finger at the 5th fret, third finger at the 7th, pinky for the 8th-fret notes.
Play low string to high, one note per beat, strict alternate picking: down, up, down, up.
The root A sits on the low E string 5th fret. That is home base - always know where it is.
Once it is clean, come straight back down from the top without stopping.
lessons.watchFor: Keep your fingers hovering close to the strings. If your pinky flies away, slow down until it stays put.

lessons.title: Finger Independence Warm-Up
lessons.summary: Not musical, but it builds the hand every other lesson depends on. Five minutes a day changes your playing.
steps: Play frets 5, 6, 7, 8 on the low E with fingers 1, 2, 3, 4 - one finger per fret.
Move to the A string and repeat. Work across all six strings.
Leave each finger down until you have to move it. That is the whole exercise.
Start at 70 BPM. Only speed up when nothing buzzes.
lessons.watchFor: The pinky is weak for everyone at first. Do not skip it or compensate with your ring finger.

lessons.title: Classic Blues Lick in A
lessons.summary: A phrase built from Box 1 that sounds like a finished musical idea, not an exercise.
steps: Start on the G string 7th fret and bend up a full step - the pitch should match the 9th fret.
Release the bend, then pick the 5th fret on the same string.
Move to the D string 7th fret, then the 5th.
Land on the A string 7th fret and let it ring. That root is what makes the phrase resolve.
lessons.watchFor: The bend is the whole lick. Stack three fingers behind each other for strength and check the pitch against the 9th fret.

lessons.title: Connecting Box 1 and Box 2
lessons.summary: Most players get stuck in one box forever. This is the move that unlocks the rest of the neck.
steps: Play Box 1 from the 5th fret up to the B string.
Slide your first finger from the 5th fret to the 8th on the B string - that is the doorway into Box 2.
Continue the shape from the 8th fret with first and third fingers.
Come back down through the same slide so the move works in both directions.
lessons.watchFor: Slide, do not jump. Your finger should stay on the string so the shift is silent and you always know where you are.

lessons.title: Pentatonic in Groups of Three
lessons.summary: Turns a plain scale run into something deliberate. Standard vocabulary for rock lead playing.
steps: Play the first three notes of the scale, then start again from the second note.
Keep strict alternate picking - the pattern makes your picking hand cross strings in new places.
Start slow enough that every note rings clearly, then push 5 BPM at a time.
lessons.watchFor: The temptation is to rush. If notes slur together, drop the tempo until each one speaks.

lessons.title: Targeting Chord Tones
lessons.summary: The difference between running scales and actually soloing. Land on the right note at the right moment.
steps: Find the chord tones of Am7 inside the scale: A, C, E and G.
Play the scale but make sure a chord tone lands on beats 1 and 3.
Use the notes in between purely as movement, never as a landing place.
Roll the dice, pick a chord, and use the coloured dots - they mark exactly these notes.
lessons.watchFor: If a phrase sounds wrong, check where it lands, not what it passes through. Landing notes carry the sound.

lessons.title: Legato Runs and Rolling Position
lessons.summary: Fewer picked notes, more flowing sound. This is how fast lines stay smooth instead of sounding hammered.
steps: Pick only the first note of each string. Everything after it is a hammer-on or pull-off.
Hammer hard from the knuckle, not the fingertip, so volume matches the picked note.
Pull off sideways, snagging the string slightly - do not just lift the finger.
Build the run across three strings without a single extra pick stroke.
lessons.watchFor: Uneven volume gives legato away. Record yourself: if the hammered notes are quieter, the technique needs more work, not more speed.

lessons.title: Power Chords and Clean Shifts
lessons.summary: Two fingers, one shape, the backbone of rock rhythm. The skill is the move between them.
steps: Fret the low E with your first finger, the A string two frets higher with your third.
Strike only those two strings. Rest your palm lightly on the strings you are not using.
Play E5, slide the shape to the 3rd fret for G5, then the 5th for A5.
Move on the beat before the change so you arrive exactly in time.
lessons.watchFor: Ringing extra strings is the usual problem. Let the underside of your first finger mute the strings above.

lessons.title: Palm Muting and Downstrokes
lessons.summary: The chug behind every rock and metal riff. It is a hand position, not a strumming pattern.
steps: Rest the edge of your picking palm on the strings right where they meet the bridge.
Too far forward kills the note, too far back does nothing. Find the spot that still has pitch.
Play all downstrokes on the low E, steady eighth notes.
Lift the palm for one beat, then put it back, so you hear the difference clearly.
lessons.watchFor: Your wrist will get tired at first - that is normal and it passes. Stop if you feel it in your forearm instead.

lessons.title: The F Barre Chord
lessons.summary: The chord that stops most players. Once the shape works, it slides anywhere on the neck.
steps: Lay your first finger flat across all six strings at the 1st fret, rolled slightly onto its bony side.
Add an E-major shape with fingers two, three and four above the barre.
Pick each string one at a time. Find which ones buzz and fix them before strumming.
Slide the whole shape to the 3rd fret and it becomes G. Same shape, new chord.
lessons.watchFor: Squeezing harder rarely fixes it. Drop your thumb down behind the neck and pull back with your arm instead.

lessons.title: A-Shape Barre and Moving Between Shapes
lessons.summary: Two barre shapes cover every chord on the neck. Switching between them is the real skill.
steps: Barre the 2nd fret with your first finger, then form an A-minor shape above it - that is Bm.
Move to the E-shape barre at the same fret for B major, and hear the difference.
Practise Bm to E to A, keeping your first finger flat and dragging it along the neck.
Never lift the barre finger fully between chords - slide it.
lessons.watchFor: If the high E string chokes on the A-shape, roll your third finger slightly flatter or mute that string deliberately.

lessons.title: Sixteenth-Note Funk Muting
lessons.summary: The strumming hand never stops moving. Notes appear only when the fretting hand allows them.
steps: Keep your strumming hand moving in constant sixteenths, down-up-down-up, sounding or not.
Release fretting-hand pressure between hits so the strum becomes a percussive click.
Press down only on the beats you want to hear. Start with beat 1 and the and of 2.
Build the groove up from the muted clicks, not down from the chords.
lessons.watchFor: If it sounds stiff, your strumming hand stopped. It should swing like a pendulum the whole bar.

lessons.title: Chord Embellishment with Suspensions
lessons.summary: Adding movement inside a chord instead of changing chord. This is what makes simple parts sound written.
steps: Hold a D chord. Add your pinky to the 3rd fret of the high E - that is Dsus4.
Lift the pinky back to D, then lift your middle finger for Dsus2.
Keep strumming through the whole move so the chord never stops ringing.
Apply the same idea to A and E shapes once it is comfortable.
lessons.watchFor: Only the moving finger should move. If the whole chord shifts, anchor your first finger harder.

lessons.title: Jazz-Blues Turnaround
lessons.summary: Four bars that show up in a thousand standards. Learn it and you can sit in with almost anyone.
steps: Use rootless voicings on the middle four strings - let a bass player cover the root.
Bb7 to Eb9 moves by only one or two notes. Find the smallest possible shift.
Comp on beats 2 and 4, not on every beat.
End on the V chord so the phrase wants to start over.
lessons.watchFor: Jazz comping is about space. If you are playing on every beat, you are playing too much.

lessons.title: G to C to D Changes
lessons.summary: Three chords that between them cover a huge number of songs. The value is changing cleanly.
steps: Fret G major and pick each string to check every note rings.
Change to C. Your third finger can stay on the A string - use it as an anchor.
Change to D, keeping the shape compact on the top three strings.
Loop G to C to D to G, one strum per chord, slowly, counting out loud.
lessons.watchFor: Move all fingers at the same time, not one after another. Practise the change without strumming first.

lessons.title: The Strumming Pattern That Fits Everything
lessons.summary: Down, down-up, up-down-up. Learn this one properly and you can play along with most songs.
steps: Keep your hand moving down and up continuously in eighth notes, like a pendulum.
Hit the strings on: beat 1 down, beat 2 down-up, then up on the and of 3, down-up on 4.
On the strums you skip, your hand still moves - it just misses the strings.
Count out loud: one, two-and, and-four-and. Say it before you play it.
lessons.watchFor: Everyone tenses up and stops the hand on skipped strums. Keep the arm swinging even when nothing sounds.

lessons.title: Travis Picking Pattern
lessons.summary: Thumb keeps a steady alternating bass while the fingers play melody on top. Sounds like two guitarists.
steps: Thumb alternates between the A string and the D string, steady as a metronome, on every beat.
Get the thumb pattern looping comfortably on its own before adding anything.
Add your index finger on the G string, landing between the thumb notes.
Add your middle finger on the B string. Keep that thumb absolutely steady - it is the anchor.
lessons.watchFor: If the thumb stumbles when the fingers join in, go back to thumb only. Independence builds slowly.

lessons.title: Using a Capo to Change Key
lessons.summary: The shapes you already know, in every key a singer might need. Ten minutes to learn, useful forever.
steps: Clamp the capo just behind the fret, not on top of it, or the strings buzz.
Put it at the 2nd fret and play G shapes - you are now in A.
Every fret you move up raises the key by a semitone. Third fret makes G shapes sound as Bb.
Retune after fitting a capo. It pulls the strings sharp, especially on cheaper guitars.
lessons.watchFor: A capo too far from the fret buzzes; too tight bends the strings sharp. Snug and close is right.

lessons.title: Fingerstyle in Drop D
lessons.summary: Tune the low E down to D and the guitar rings in a way standard tuning cannot match.
steps: Tune the low E down until it matches the open D string, one octave lower. The tuner in Tools shows you when.
Let the low D ring as a drone underneath everything you play.
Pick the melody on the top strings and let open strings sustain into each other.
Avoid damping. The overlap between notes is the entire point of this tuning.
lessons.watchFor: Check tuning often - a freshly dropped string drifts, and the drone exposes it instantly.

lessons.title: Percussive Slap and Body Hits
lessons.summary: Turns one guitar into a guitar and a drummer. The move behind most modern acoustic playing.
steps: On beats 2 and 4, bring the heel of your strumming hand down onto the strings over the soundhole.
The strings should stop dead and thump. That is your snare.
Keep the chord fretted the whole time so the slap has pitch behind it.
Alternate: strum, slap, strum, slap - until the slap lands without you thinking about it.
lessons.watchFor: Hit with a relaxed hand. Tensing up makes a slapping noise with no body behind it, and hurts after a while.

lessons.title: Natural Harmonics and Open Tuning Textures
lessons.summary: The bell-like tones behind a lot of modern acoustic music. Easy to touch, hard to place well.
steps: Rest a finger lightly directly over the 12th fret wire - do not press down.
Pick the string and lift the finger at the same moment. You get a chime an octave up.
The 7th and 5th frets give higher harmonics. The 5th is the hardest to get cleanly.
Work them into a picked passage rather than playing them on their own.
lessons.watchFor: Exactly over the fret wire, not behind it. A millimetre off and you get a dead thud instead of a chime.

lessons.title: Rock Double Stops
lessons.summary: Two notes at once. The sound behind Chuck Berry, AC/DC and half of rock rhythm-lead playing.
steps: Fret the G and B strings at the same fret with your first finger, or one finger each.
Strike both strings together with a single downstroke.
Slide the pair from the 5th fret to the 7th and back without lifting.
Bend the lower of the two notes slightly while the upper rings - that is the classic sound.
lessons.watchFor: Both notes must speak equally. If one is quiet, flatten the finger slightly and pick closer to the bridge.

lessons.title: The Blues Curl and Vibrato
lessons.summary: A quarter-tone bend that lands between happy and sad. This one detail separates blues from rock phrasing.
steps: Fret the G string 5th fret and push the string just slightly - less than a semitone.
You are aiming for the note between minor and major third. It should sound almost out of tune.
Hold it there, then add vibrato by rocking your wrist, not your finger.
Release slowly. The whole gesture is one expression, not two moves.
lessons.watchFor: Vibrato comes from wrist rotation with your thumb anchored. Finger-wiggling vibrato sounds nervous.

lessons.title: Alternate Picking Speed Bursts
lessons.summary: Controlled bursts train speed better than playing fast badly for an hour.
steps: Play four fast sixteenth notes, then rest for a full beat. That is one burst.
The rest matters as much as the notes - it lets the hand reset instead of tensing.
Keep the pick angle shallow and move from the wrist, never the elbow.
Add one burst per bar until you can chain four together cleanly.
lessons.watchFor: If your forearm burns, you are gripping too hard. The pick should feel almost loose between your fingers.

lessons.title: Bebop Enclosures
lessons.summary: Surround the target note from above and below before landing on it. The core of jazz line construction.
steps: Pick your target - the 3rd of the chord, F over Dm7.
Play the note a semitone above it, then the note a tone below, then land on the target.
That three-note wrap is an enclosure. It works into any chord tone.
Chain two enclosures together to build a full bar of line.
lessons.watchFor: The enclosure must resolve on a strong beat or it just sounds wrong instead of intentional.

lessons.title: Melodic Fills Between Vocal Lines
lessons.summary: Lead playing that supports a song instead of competing with it. Space is the technique.
steps: Play only in the gaps - the last two beats of a four-bar phrase.
Use notes from the chord that is sounding, not a scale run.
Two or three notes is a fill. Eight is a solo, and it will bury the singer.
End the fill on the root of the next chord so it hands back cleanly.
lessons.watchFor: The instinct is to fill every gap. Leave some empty - it makes the ones you play matter.

lessons.title: Funk Lead in the Dorian Box
lessons.summary: Short, rhythmic, percussive. Funk lead is closer to drumming than to singing.
steps: Stay in one position. Movement up the neck kills the groove.
Play in bursts of two or three notes, always landing on the and of a beat.
Mute aggressively between phrases - silence is part of the rhythm.
Use the 6th of the scale (B over Dm) constantly. It is the Dorian sound.
lessons.watchFor: If it sounds like a rock solo, your notes are too long. Cut every note in half.

lessons.title: Harmonic Minor Sweep Shapes
lessons.summary: The scale and the sweep that define neo-classical playing. Both need to be exact or it collapses.
steps: Harmonic minor is the natural minor with a raised 7th. That one note is the whole flavour.
For the sweep, the pick moves in one continuous direction across the strings.
Each finger lifts the instant the next lands - only one note may ring at a time.
Play it as slow arpeggios first. If notes bleed together at slow speed, speed will not fix it.
lessons.watchFor: Bleeding notes are the giveaway. Mute with the fretting finger as it lifts, not with your palm.

lessons.title: The Driving Eighth-Note Riff
lessons.summary: All downstrokes, no let-up. It is a stamina exercise disguised as a riff.
steps: Every eighth note is a downstroke. No upstrokes at all - that is what makes it drive.
Palm mute the low notes and lift the mute for accents.
Keep the picking arm moving from the elbow with a loose wrist.
Two bars of E5, two of A5. Do not slow down at the change.
lessons.watchFor: Your arm will tire before your fretting hand. Build up in two-minute stretches rather than pushing through.

lessons.title: The 12-Bar Shuffle
lessons.summary: The form behind thousands of songs. Learn the shape of it and you can play blues with strangers.
steps: Bars 1-4 stay on A7. Bars 5-6 go to D7, then back to A7 for 7-8.
Bar 9 is E7, bar 10 D7, bar 11 A7, bar 12 E7 to turn it around.
Play a shuffle rhythm: long-short, long-short, like a limp rather than an even beat.
Count the bars out loud until the form is automatic.
lessons.watchFor: The shuffle feel is the hard part, not the chords. If it sounds like straight eighths, exaggerate the long-short.

lessons.title: Gallop Rhythm and Tight Muting
lessons.summary: One eighth plus two sixteenths, over and over. The engine of thrash and heavy metal rhythm.
steps: The pattern is down, down-up: one long, two short. Say "dum-diddy" out loud.
Palm mute all of it. The mute must stay locked in the same place the whole time.
Every note must have identical length and volume, or the gallop turns to mush.
Start at 90 BPM and only move up when it is machine-even.
lessons.watchFor: Uneven sixteenths are the usual failure. Record it and listen back - your ears lie in real time.

lessons.title: Freddie Green Comping
lessons.summary: Four beats to the bar, tiny voicings, no sustain. The invisible engine of big band guitar.
steps: Use only three notes per chord, on the middle strings. Anything more clutters the band.
Play one strum per beat, all downstrokes, and cut each one short.
The chord should sound for about a quarter of the beat - it is percussion with pitch.
Keep the volume even. No accents, no dynamics, just relentless pulse.
lessons.watchFor: Ringing chords is the mistake. Release fretting pressure right after each strum to choke it.

lessons.title: Bass-Strum Alternating Pattern
lessons.summary: Thumb plays the root, then the hand strums the top. One guitar sounding like a band.
steps: On beat 1, pick only the root note of the chord on a bass string.
On beat 2, strum the top three or four strings.
On beat 3, pick a different chord tone in the bass - the fifth works well.
On beat 4, strum the top again. Loop it and change chords without breaking the pattern.
lessons.watchFor: The bass note must be a single string. If you catch neighbours, angle the pick and aim smaller.

lessons.title: The Ninth-Chord Stab
lessons.summary: One chord, played rhythmically enough to carry an entire song.
steps: Fret E9 on the middle four strings and mute everything else with your first finger.
Strum only sixteenths, hand never stopping, sounding maybe three hits per bar.
The rest of the strums are dead - fretting hand releases so they click.
Put your hits on the and of 2 and the and of 4 to start. Move them once it locks.
lessons.watchFor: Funk lives or dies on the muted strums. If they are silent instead of clicking, press less but keep contact.

lessons.title: Pedal Point and Diminished Movement
lessons.summary: One note stays fixed while the harmony climbs over it. Baroque device, metal application.
steps: Keep the open A string ringing as the pedal on every beat.
Between each pedal note, play a rising chord tone on the higher strings.
Move through Am, then a diminished chord, then E - the tension builds against the fixed bass.
Alternate-pick strictly so the pedal note never loses volume.
lessons.watchFor: The pedal must stay perfectly even. If it fluctuates, the whole effect falls apart.

lessons.title: Driving Acoustic Rhythm
lessons.summary: How to make an acoustic cut through without a band behind it. Attack and control.
steps: Strum from the elbow with more force than usual, but keep the wrist loose.
Accent beats 2 and 4 hard - that is what makes it feel like a drum kit is there.
Mute the strings with your palm on the off-beats for a percussive gap.
Play near the bridge for bite, over the soundhole for warmth. Move between them.
lessons.watchFor: Hitting harder makes it louder, not better. Past a point the strings just rattle - find that ceiling and stay under it.

lessons.title: Delta Blues Thumb and Slide
lessons.summary: The oldest sound on the instrument. Steady thumb, moaning slide over the top.
steps: Thumb keeps a dead-steady bass on the low strings, never varying.
Wear the slide on your third or fourth finger, resting fingers behind it to damp noise.
Rest the slide directly over the fret wire - not behind it - and use no pressure at all.
Slide into notes from a fret or two below rather than landing on them.
lessons.watchFor: Fingers behind the slide are what stop the rattle. Without them it is all noise and no note.

lessons.title: Dark Fingerstyle in Drop D
lessons.summary: Heavy writing without distortion. The intro to a lot of metal albums lives here.
steps: Drop the low E to D and let it drone under everything.
Use the flat second - Eb over D - for the phrygian darkness.
Pick with your fingertips, not nails, for a duller and heavier tone.
Let notes overlap and clash slightly. The dissonance is the point.
lessons.watchFor: Do not rush it. This style depends on space and decay, and speed kills both.

lessons.title: Chord Melody Basics
lessons.summary: Melody and chords at the same time, from one guitar. The hardest and most rewarding acoustic skill.
steps: Put the melody note on the top string, always. It must be the highest note you play.
Build the chord underneath it using only two or three more notes.
Drop notes freely - the fifth is almost always expendable.
Work one bar at a time. Two bars a day is real progress here.
lessons.watchFor: If the melody is not clearly the loudest note, the arrangement fails no matter how good the chords are.

lessons.title: Acoustic Funk Scratch
lessons.summary: Percussion first, chord second. The acoustic can groove if you stop treating it as a strummer.
steps: Fret Am7 but release the pressure so no note rings - just deadened strings.
Strum sixteenths and listen to the scratch. That rhythm is the foundation.
Press down for one or two hits per bar to let the chord flash through.
Keep the strumming hand identical whether notes sound or not.
lessons.watchFor: Both hands are doing separate jobs. Practise the strumming hand alone first, then add the fretting hand.

lessons.title: Classical Right-Hand Arpeggios
lessons.summary: The p-i-m-a pattern behind classical guitar. Precise, even, and it transfers to everything else.
steps: Thumb (p) takes the bass string. Index, middle and ring (i, m, a) take strings 3, 2 and 1.
Play p-i-m-a as a rolling arpeggio, one finger per note, never repeating a finger in a row.
Plant the next finger on its string before the previous note finishes.
Every note must be identical in volume. That evenness is the entire exercise.
lessons.watchFor: The ring finger is weakest and will be quiet. Practise a-m-i on its own until it matches.

lessons.title: Fingerpicking a Folk Ballad
lessons.summary: The gentle rolling pattern behind countless folk songs. Slow, simple, and it sounds finished immediately.
steps: Thumb plays the root of the chord on beat 1, every bar, without fail.
Index picks the G string, middle picks the B string, in a steady roll after it.
Keep the pattern identical through every chord change - only the left hand moves.
Let every note ring. Nothing gets damped in this style.
lessons.watchFor: Changing the picking pattern at each chord is the common error. The pattern stays; the chord moves underneath it.

lessons.title: Chicken Pickin Basics
lessons.summary: That snappy, popping country lead sound. It comes from the picking hand, not the notes.
steps: Hold the pick normally, but let your middle finger sit under the string as well.
Pick a note downward, then snap the next one upward with that middle finger so it pops off the fretboard.
Alternate pick and finger. The finger notes should be noticeably louder and sharper.
Add a light palm mute to the picked notes so the popped ones jump out even more.
lessons.watchFor: The pop comes from pulling the string away from the neck and letting it slap back, not from picking harder.

lessons.title: Pedal Steel Bends
lessons.summary: Making a guitar cry like a pedal steel. Two notes, one bending into the other while both ring.
steps: Fret the B string 8th fret and the high E 7th fret at the same time.
Bend only the B string up a full step while the high E stays exactly where it is.
Both notes must ring through the whole bend - that clash resolving is the steel sound.
Hold at the top for a beat before releasing, and keep the static note steady.
lessons.watchFor: The unbent note usually gets pulled sharp or muted. Keep that finger firm and independent of the bending one.

lessons.title: The Boom-Chick Rhythm
lessons.summary: Bass note, then chord. The heartbeat of country rhythm guitar since the beginning.
steps: On beats 1 and 3, pick just the root note of the chord on a bass string - that is the boom.
On beats 2 and 4, strum the top three or four strings short and clipped - that is the chick.
Alternate the bass between the root and the fifth so it walks instead of repeating.
Keep the chick strums tight and muted. They are percussion, not chords.
lessons.watchFor: If the chick rings out, it turns into folk strumming. Choke it with your palm right after the strum.

lessons.title: Walking Bass Runs Between Chords
lessons.summary: The little bass lines that connect chords. It is what makes country rhythm sound alive instead of blocky.
steps: Play the last two beats of a bar as single bass notes instead of a strum.
Walk from the root of the chord you are on to the root of the chord coming next.
From G to C, walk G-A-B-C on the low strings. Use the scale, step by step.
Land exactly on beat 1 of the new chord. The run must arrive on time or it fails.
lessons.watchFor: Runs that arrive late are worse than no run at all. Practise just the last beat and the landing.

lessons.title: Carter Family Picking
lessons.summary: Melody on the bass strings with strums between. The original country guitar style.
steps: Pick the melody with your thumb on the bottom three strings.
Between each melody note, brush the top strings lightly with your fingers.
The melody must stay louder than the brushes - it is the tune, they are accompaniment.
Keep the thumb strictly in time. The brushes fill the gaps, they do not set the pace.
lessons.watchFor: Brushing too hard buries the melody. It should feel like a whisper between the thumb notes.

lessons.title: Your First Bend
lessons.summary: Bending is what makes a guitar sing instead of just sounding notes. Get it in tune from day one.
steps: Fret the G string 7th fret with your third finger. Put your first and second fingers behind it on the same string.
Push the string toward the ceiling using your wrist rotating, not your fingertip pushing.
Aim for the pitch of the 9th fret. Play the 9th first so your ear knows the target.
Hold at the top for a full beat, then lower it back down under control.
lessons.watchFor: Almost everyone bends flat at first. Check against the target fret every single time until your hand learns the distance.

lessons.title: Hammer-Ons and Pull-Offs
lessons.summary: Two notes for one pick stroke. The foundation of every smooth, flowing lead line.
steps: Pick the 5th fret on the B string, then slam your third finger onto the 7th without picking again.
Hammer from the knuckle so the note is as loud as the picked one.
For the pull-off, start with both fingers down. Pick the 7th, then pull the finger off sideways so it snags the string.
Loop hammer, pull, hammer, pull on one string until both notes match in volume.
lessons.watchFor: Lifting straight up gives you a dead note. The pull-off is a small sideways flick, almost like a tiny pick stroke.

lessons.title: Simple Riff Building
lessons.summary: Four notes, arranged well, is a riff. This is how you write one instead of noodling.
steps: Pick three or four notes from the scale and nothing else. Fewer notes forces better choices.
Play them in a rhythm you can clap. If you cannot clap it, it is not a riff yet.
Repeat it exactly the same way four times so the ear learns it.
Change only the last note the fourth time round. That small change is what makes it feel finished.
lessons.watchFor: The temptation is to keep adding notes. Resist it - the best riffs are almost embarrassingly simple.

lessons.title: String Skipping for Wide Intervals
lessons.summary: Skipping strings turns a predictable scale run into something that sounds composed.
steps: Play a note on the low E, then jump straight to the D string, missing the A entirely.
Mute the skipped string with the underside of your fretting finger so it never sounds.
Keep the picking hand travelling in a straight line - do not swing around the missed string.
Build a four-note pattern that skips once, then move it up the neck.
lessons.watchFor: The skipped string ringing is the whole difficulty. If you hear it, your muting finger is not flat enough.

lessons.title: Two-Hand Tapping
lessons.summary: The right hand joins the fretboard. Wide intervals no single hand could reach.
steps: Fret the 5th fret on the B string with your first finger and the 8th with your third.
Tap the 12th fret with your picking-hand index finger, hard, straight down.
Pull that finger off sideways to sound the 8th, then pull off again to the 5th.
Loop tap-pull-pull as one continuous triplet. Keep the tapping finger close to the string.
lessons.watchFor: Rest your picking-hand palm on the lower strings while tapping or the whole guitar rings with noise.

lessons.title: Reading and Feeling 4/4
lessons.summary: Before any strumming pattern works, the count has to be automatic. Ten minutes here saves months.
steps: Count one, two, three, four out loud with the metronome, over and over.
Strum once on beat 1 only. Let the other three beats pass in silence.
Now strum on 1 and 3. Then on 2 and 4 - that is the backbeat, where a snare drum lands.
Only once those are locked, strum all four.
lessons.watchFor: If you speed up when you get excited, you have not internalised the beat yet. The metronome is the referee.

lessons.title: Chord Inversions and Slash Chords
lessons.summary: Same chord, different bass note. It turns a blocky progression into a moving bass line.
steps: Play a C chord, then move the bass note to E on the low E string 7th fret - that is C/E.
The chord has not changed, only which note is lowest.
Going C to C/E to F gives you a bass line walking C, E, F while the chord barely moves.
Look for the smallest bass move between any two chords and use an inversion to get it.
lessons.watchFor: The bass note must be the lowest thing sounding. If you accidentally hit a lower string, the effect vanishes.

lessons.title: Dynamics: Playing Quiet on Purpose
lessons.summary: Volume control is a rhythm technique. A part played quietly makes the loud part actually feel loud.
steps: Play the progression as softly as you can while every string still rings clearly.
Play it again at full force. Notice how much range you actually have.
Now do four bars quiet, four bars loud, without changing the pattern at all.
Move the pick closer to the neck for softer and warmer, nearer the bridge for harder and brighter.
lessons.watchFor: Quiet does not mean sloppy. The soft version needs the same accuracy, just less force.

lessons.title: Syncopation and Off-Beat Accents
lessons.summary: Putting the emphasis where the beat is not. This is what makes a riff feel like it pushes.
steps: Count one-and-two-and-three-and-four-and out loud, evenly.
Play only on the "ands" - never on a numbered beat. It will feel wrong at first.
Now add a hit on beat 1 to anchor it, keeping the rest on the offbeats.
Palm mute the anchor and let the offbeats ring so the contrast is obvious.
lessons.watchFor: Most players drift back onto the beat within two bars. Keep counting out loud until you do not.

lessons.title: Chord Substitution in a Progression
lessons.summary: Swapping one chord for another that does the same job. How jazz players make standards their own.
steps: Any chord can be replaced by one sharing two or more notes with it.
Cmaj7 and Em7 share three notes - swap them and the progression still works but the colour shifts.
Replace a dominant 7th with the chord a tritone away: G7 becomes Db7, and the bass slides chromatically.
Change one chord at a time and listen. Two at once and you cannot hear what did what.
lessons.watchFor: Substitutions must still resolve. If the ear feels lost rather than surprised, you went one step too far.

lessons.title: Reading a Chord Diagram
lessons.summary: Five minutes that unlocks every chord book, website and app you will ever use, including this one.
steps: The six vertical lines are the strings, low E on the left, high e on the right.
Horizontal lines are frets. The thick line at the top is the nut - the end of the neck.
A dot means press there. A number in the dot is the note name.
An x above a string means do not play it. An o means play it open, unfretted.
lessons.watchFor: Diagrams are drawn as if the guitar is standing up facing you - not as you look down at it. That flip confuses everyone at first.

lessons.title: Hybrid Picking
lessons.summary: Pick and fingers together. You get the attack of a pick with the independence of fingerstyle.
steps: Hold the pick normally between thumb and index.
Your middle and ring fingers are now free to pluck the top two strings.
Pick the bass note with the pick, then pluck two higher strings together with the fingers.
That pick-then-pluck motion is the whole technique. Loop it through a chord change.
lessons.watchFor: The plucked notes usually come out louder than you expect. Ease off with the fingers until they sit level with the pick.

lessons.title: Open D Tuning
lessons.summary: Retune and the open strings become a chord. Everything you know shifts, and the guitar rings differently.
steps: Tune to D-A-D-F#-A-D. Drop strings 1, 2 and 6 - use the tuner in Tools.
Strum all six open strings. That is a full D major with no fretting at all.
Barre straight across any fret with one finger and you get another major chord.
Let open strings ring against fretted notes - that clash and resolve is why this tuning exists.
lessons.watchFor: Retuning changes string tension, so check every string twice. The first tuning pass will already be out by the time you finish it.

lessons.title: Writing a Melody Over Your Chords
lessons.summary: The last step. You have chords and scales - this turns them into something someone could sing.
steps: Loop your progression until it is automatic and you can stop thinking about the chords.
Hum a line over it before you play a single note. Your voice will not choose anything unmusical.
Find the hummed notes on the fretboard. They will almost always be chord tones on the strong beats.
Leave gaps. A melody that never breathes is exhausting to listen to and impossible to sing.
lessons.watchFor: Playing before humming is the trap - your hands go to comfortable shapes rather than good melodies. Voice first, always.

lessons.title: Fingerstyle Blues Bass and Melody
lessons.summary: Thumb plays the shuffle, fingers answer it. One guitar covering both jobs.
steps: Thumb plays a steady alternating bass on the low E and A strings, in a long-short shuffle.
Get the thumb going alone until it needs no thought at all.
Add single melody notes on the top strings between thumb strokes.
Bend the G string slightly during the gaps - the bass never pauses for it.
lessons.watchFor: The thumb is the drummer and it must not react to what the fingers do. If the bass stumbles, drop the melody.

lessons.title: Finding Any Note on the Neck
lessons.summary: Stop guessing where notes are. Two strings memorised unlocks the whole fretboard.
steps: Learn the low E string first: open E, 1st F, 3rd G, 5th A, 7th B, 8th C, 10th D, 12th E.
Say each note out loud as you play it. Saying it is what makes it stick.
Do the same on the A string: open A, 2nd B, 3rd C, 5th D, 7th E, 8th F, 10th G.
Now any barre chord root can be found instantly, because those two strings carry them.
lessons.watchFor: Do five minutes daily rather than an hour once. This is memorisation, and memorisation needs repetition, not intensity.

lessons.title: Mixing Major and Minor Pentatonic
lessons.summary: The trick behind almost every great blues solo: refusing to pick a side.
steps: Play A minor pentatonic at the 5th fret until it is comfortable.
Now play A major pentatonic - same shape moved down three frets, to the 2nd.
Alternate: one phrase minor, next phrase major, over the same A7 chord.
The magic note is the minor 3rd sliding into the major 3rd. Find it and lean on it.
lessons.watchFor: Switching mid-phrase sounds like a mistake. Switch between phrases, where the ear expects a new idea.

lessons.title: Playing Over Changes, Not Through Them
lessons.summary: Most players run one scale over everything. This is how you make each chord audible.
steps: Over Dm7 target F and C. Over G7 target B and F. Over Cmaj7 target E and B.
Play only those two notes per chord at first, in time. It will already sound like jazz.
Now connect them with scale notes, still landing on the targets.
The B to F on the G7 is the tritone - it is what makes the chord want to resolve.
lessons.watchFor: If it sounds like one scale over three chords, your landing notes are not changing. Slow down and check each one.

lessons.title: Muting Strings You Are Not Playing
lessons.summary: Clean playing is mostly about silence. This is the skill nobody teaches beginners.
steps: Fret a power chord on the A and D strings.
Let the tip of your first finger lean against the low E so it cannot ring.
Rest the underside of the same finger flat against the G, B and high E.
Strum all six strings hard. Only two should sound. That is the goal.
lessons.watchFor: If stray strings ring, you are pressing with the very tip. Flatten the finger slightly so more of it touches.

lessons.title: Two-Beat Country Feel
lessons.summary: The bounce behind classic country rhythm. It sits on 1 and 3, and it never rushes.
steps: Bass note on beat 1, chord chop on beat 2. Repeat on 3 and 4.
The chop must be short - kill it immediately with your palm.
Keep the bass notes walking between root and fifth so it moves.
Play it with a metronome on 2 and 4 only. If you drift, you will hear it instantly.
lessons.watchFor: Country rhythm is felt, not rushed. If it speeds up, the whole band sounds nervous.

lessons.title: The One - Locking to the Downbeat
lessons.summary: Everything in funk points at beat one. Miss it and nothing else matters.
steps: Play a single hard accent on beat 1 of every bar and nothing else. Four bars.
Now add muted sixteenths between, keeping beat 1 the loudest thing by far.
Drop notes anywhere except beat 1 - the groove survives.
Drop beat 1 and it collapses. That is the lesson.
lessons.watchFor: Accenting everything means accenting nothing. The one has to be noticeably louder.

lessons.title: Changing Chords Without Stopping
lessons.summary: The single biggest beginner frustration, and it has a specific fix.
steps: Pick two chords and play four beats of each, over and over.
On beat 4, lift your fingers and move - do not wait until beat 1.
Arriving early is fine. Arriving late breaks the song.
If you cannot make it, slow the metronome until you can. Speed comes free later.
lessons.watchFor: Everyone tries to hold the chord until the last instant. Leave early, arrive ready.

lessons.title: Alternate Bass with Chord Changes
lessons.summary: Once the thumb pattern works on one chord, this is how you carry it through a song.
steps: Every chord has a root and a fifth. Find both in the bass strings for each shape.
C: root on A string 3rd fret, fifth on low E 3rd fret. Am: root A open, fifth E open.
Alternate root-fifth-root-fifth under every chord, without breaking the pattern.
The chord changes above; the thumb never notices.
lessons.watchFor: The pattern must not reset at each chord. Practise the thumb alone through the changes first.

lessons.title: Walking Bass Under Chords
lessons.summary: Bass line and chords at once. It sounds like a duo and it is one of the most useful acoustic skills.
steps: Thumb walks quarter notes on the bass strings - root, approach, root of the next chord.
Chords land on the offbeats, in between the bass notes, kept small and quiet.
Approach each new root from a half step above or below. That is what makes it walk.
Bass first, always. Add the chords only when the walk is steady.
lessons.watchFor: The bass must stay perfectly even. If it hesitates when a chord lands, drop the chords and rebuild.

lessons.title: Alternating Bass Pedal with Arpeggios
lessons.summary: Baroque device, metal execution. One hand holds the ground while the other climbs.
steps: Low A rings on every downbeat as the pedal, struck with a downstroke every time.
Between pedals, arpeggiate Am, then the diminished, then E, on the top strings.
Use strict alternate picking so the pedal never loses volume.
Build the tension across four bars, then resolve to Am and let it ring.
lessons.watchFor: The pedal is the whole effect. If it weakens as the arpeggios get busy, slow down until it does not.
